cards.name: The Fed's rate
cards.what: This is the overnight rate the Fed sets for banks, and most busts begin with the Fed raising it while a boom is still running.
cards.reading: Up 0.25 points over the last six months
cards.rule: It counts as fired once the Fed has raised in the last six months without cutting since, and as warming if the rate is simply higher than a year ago.
cards.history: In the two years before each top, the Fed's rate went from 5.75% to 5.98% in 2000, from 3.73% to 4.91% in 2007, and from 1.42% to 1.59% in 2020.
cards.trigger: fires on a hike in the last six months with no cut since

cards.name: Long-term borrowing cost
cards.what: This is what the US government pays to borrow for 30 years, and when it climbs quickly, mortgages, company loans and stock prices all come under pressure.
cards.reading: Up 0.77 points from a year ago
cards.rule: It counts as fired when the yield is up three quarters of a point in a year, and as warming at a quarter point.
cards.history: Before the 1987 crash it rose from about 7.5% to over 10% in seven months, and when Britain's long bonds broke in 2022, pension funds were hit with margin calls within three days. These figures come from the project's earlier crash study and are rounded.
cards.trigger: fires at a rise of three quarters of a point in a year

cards.name: The yield curve
cards.what: This is the 10-year Treasury rate minus the 3-month rate. It drops below zero when the bond market expects trouble, and the crash has usually come after it climbs back above zero rather than while it's negative.
cards.reading: Back above zero since Oct 2025, after 36 months below it
cards.rule: It counts as warming while it's below zero, and as fired once it's back above zero within two years of a long stretch below, which is the window where recessions have usually begun.
cards.history: It was below zero from Apr 2000 to Feb 2001 around the Mar 2000 top, from Jul 2006 to Aug 2007 ahead of the Oct 2007 top, and from Mar 2019 to Oct 2019 ahead of the Feb 2020 top.
cards.trigger: fires when it climbs back above zero after a long inversion

cards.name: Banks getting stingy
cards.what: Every quarter the Fed asks bank loan officers whether they're making it harder for businesses to borrow, and this number is the share saying yes minus the share saying they've eased up.
cards.reading: Net share of banks tightening business-loan rules
cards.rule: It counts as fired when 20% or more of banks are tightening on net, and as warming at anything above zero.
cards.history: The net share tightening was 11% at the 2000 top before climbing to 60%, 19% at the 2007 top before climbing to 84%, and 0% at the 2020 top before climbing to 71%. The survey comes out quarterly, and the next one is due in early February.
cards.source_label: FRED DRTSCILM, Fed loan officer survey
cards.trigger: fires at 20% tightening

cards.name: Tech leaders vs the whole market
cards.what: The Nasdaq-100 holds the giant companies that led the boom, and in a mania they tend to fall first while the broader S&P 500 hides the damage.
cards.reading: The Nasdaq-100 is 11% below its Oct 6, 2026 high, while the S&P 500 is only 3% below its own
cards.rule: It counts as fired when the Nasdaq-100 is 15% or more below its high of the past year, and as warming at 8%.
cards.history: From March to May 2000 the Nasdaq-100 fell 36%, yet on Sept 1 the S&P 500 fund was only 1% below its high. It went on to fall 54% from the 2007 top to the 2009 bottom, and 28% in five weeks in 2020.
cards.trigger: fires at 15% below its high

cards.name: Chip stocks, the AI leaders
cards.what: The semiconductor fund (SMH) holds Nvidia, Broadcom and the other chip makers behind the AI build-out, so it's the best single read on this boom's leaders.
cards.reading: The chip fund is 31% below its Jun 22, 2026 high, and Nvidia (NVDA) is 35% below its own
cards.rule: It counts as fired at 20% or more below its high of the past year, and as warming at 10%.
cards.history: The chip fund fell 83% from 2000 to 2002, 62% from the 2007 top, and 34% in the 2020 crash.
cards.trigger: fires at 20% below its high

cards.name: The weakest junk bonds
cards.what: CCC bonds are issued by the companies most likely to default, so the extra interest they have to pay over Treasuries tends to jump first when lenders start pulling back.
cards.reading: Points over Treasuries, up 4.78 since January and just under the Oct 23 high of 13.56, while the safest junk (BB) pays only 1.86
cards.rule: It counts as fired when the spread is up 3 points or more from its low of the past year, and as warming at 1.5.
cards.history: This pattern, with the weakest bonds blowing out while the rest of junk stays calm, showed up before 1990 and 2007, though it also gave false alarms in 1998, 2011 and 2016. That record comes from the project's earlier study, because the Fed's site now only shows three years of this series.
cards.trigger: fires at 3 points above its low of the past year

cards.name: All junk bonds
cards.what: This is the extra interest that all below-investment-grade companies pay over Treasuries, and when it widens, the whole market for risky borrowers is starting to shut.
cards.reading: Points of extra interest over Treasuries, up 0.63 from the low of the past year
cards.rule: It counts as fired at 6 points or more, and as warming at 4.5 or after a rise of 1.5 from its low of the past year.
cards.history: From memory and rounded, it sat around 2.4 at the 2007 low and reached about 22 at the December 2008 peak, went from about 3.5 to about 11 in March 2020, and rose from roughly 5 to around 9 during 2000. The Fed's site only shows three years now, so these can't be checked live.
cards.trigger: fires at 6 points

cards.name: Short-term company IOUs
cards.what: Commercial paper is how banks and large companies borrow for a few weeks at a time, and its gap over Treasury bills jumps when lenders stop trusting the borrowers. This was the first thing to break in August 2007.
cards.reading: Points over Treasury bills, averaged over five days
cards.rule: It counts as fired at 1 point or more, and as warming at half a point.
cards.history: The gap peaked at 1.17 in May 2000, 3.73 in Oct 2008, and 2.57 in Mar 2020.
cards.trigger: fires at 1 point

cards.name: Bank stocks
cards.what: Banks feel bad loans before anyone else, which is why their stocks usually roll over while the broader market is still near its high.
cards.reading: The bank index is 11% below its Aug 14, 2026 high, and regional banks (KRE) are 7% below theirs
cards.rule: It counts as fired at 20% or more below its high of the past year, and as warming at 10%.
cards.history: On the day the S&P 500 topped, bank stocks were already 14% below their Apr 1999 high in 2000, 9% below their Feb 2007 high in 2007, and 5% below their Jan 2020 high in 2020.
cards.source_label: KBW bank index, Yahoo Finance daily closes
cards.trigger: fires at 20% below its high

cards.name: Banks at the Fed's emergency window
cards.what: The discount window is where banks borrow from the Fed when nobody else will lend to them, so a jump in it usually means a bank is losing its funding.
cards.reading: Billions borrowed in the week of Nov 11, 2026, after $9.2 billion the week before
cards.rule: It counts as fired at $22 billion or more two weeks running, which is the project's go-time line, and as warming at $10 billion.
cards.history: It peaked at $111 billion in Oct 2008, $51 billion in Mar 2020, and $153 billion in Mar 2023, and before Silicon Valley Bank failed it had been sitting at $5 to $10 billion for 15 weeks.
cards.source_label: FRED WLCFLPCL, Fed weekly balance sheet
cards.trigger: fires at $22 billion two weeks running

cards.name: Overnight lending vs the Fed's floor
cards.what: SOFR is the cost of borrowing cash overnight against Treasuries, and when it rises above the rate the Fed pays banks on their reserves, cash is getting scarce in the system.
cards.reading: Basis points above the Fed's rate, averaged over five days (100 basis points is 1%)
cards.rule: It counts as fired at 10 basis points or more above the Fed's rate, and as warming at anything above it.
cards.history: In September 2019 overnight cash jumped to 5.25% for a day, more than double the normal rate, and the Fed had to step in. SOFR only started in 2018, so there's nothing to show for 2000 or 2008.
cards.trigger: fires at 10 basis points above the Fed's rate

cards.name: Banks borrowing from the Fed's repo desk
cards.what: This is the cash the Fed lends overnight against Treasuries, and heavy use of it means private lenders are pulling back.
cards.reading: Billions a day, averaged over five days
cards.rule: It counts as fired at $25 billion a day or more on average, and as warming at $10 billion. Spikes at the end of a month are normal, which is why it's averaged.
cards.history: It peaked at $101 billion in Mar 2020, and the Fed only restarted this tool in September 2019.
cards.trigger: fires at $25 billion a day

cards.name: Overall money conditions
cards.what: The Chicago Fed rolls 105 measures of credit, funding and markets into one number, where zero is average and anything above zero means money is tighter than normal.
cards.reading: Zero is average, and above zero is tighter than normal
cards.rule: It counts as fired above zero, and as warming above minus 0.25.
cards.history: It went from -0.11 at the 2000 top to a peak of +0.04, from +0.05 at the 2007 top to a peak of +3.11, and from -0.54 at the 2020 top to a peak of +0.18.
cards.trigger: fires above zero

cards.name: The fear gauge
cards.what: The VIX is the price of insurance on the S&P 500. It climbs on the way down rather than before, so it confirms a panic instead of warning about one.
cards.reading: The five-day average is 19.0
cards.rule: It counts as fired when the five-day average reaches 30, and as warming at 20.
cards.history: It went from 23 at the 2000 top to a peak of 45 in Aug 2002, from 16 at the 2007 top to a peak of 81 in Nov 2008, and from 14 at the 2020 top to a peak of 83 in Mar 2020.
cards.trigger: fires at a five-day average of 30

cards.name: Financial stress index
cards.what: This is the St. Louis Fed's stress gauge, built from 18 market measures, where zero is normal and anything above it means stress.
cards.reading: Zero is normal, and above zero means stress
cards.rule: It counts as fired above 1, and as warming above zero.
cards.history: It went from -0.1 at the 2000 top to a peak of +2.0, from +0.6 at the 2007 top to a peak of +9.7, and from -0.6 at the 2020 top to a peak of +5.6.
cards.trigger: fires above 1

cards.name: The yen jumps
cards.what: Traders borrow cheap yen to buy everything else, and when they're forced to sell, they have to buy the yen back, which makes it spike. A stronger yen shows up as fewer yen per dollar.
cards.reading: Yen per dollar, with the yen weaker by 1.1% over the last 20 trading days
cards.rule: It counts as fired when the yen is 7% stronger over 20 trading days, and as warming at 3%.
cards.history: The yen gained as much as 17% in October 1998, 15% in 2008, and 12% in August 2024, each within about a month. The Fed posts this series weekly, so it can trail the market by a few days.
cards.source_label: FRED DEXJPUS (Fed H.10), daily, posted weekly
cards.trigger: fires when the yen is 7% stronger in a month

cards.name: The job market cracks
cards.what: The Sahm rule says a recession has started once the three-month average jobless rate is half a point above its low of the past year. It confirms a downturn late rather than warning early.
cards.reading: Points above the low of the past year
cards.rule: It counts as fired at 0.5 or more, and as warming at 0.3.
cards.history: It crossed 0.5 in Jun 2001, 14 months after the 2000 top; in Apr 2008, 6 months after the 2007 top; and in Apr 2020, 1 month after the 2020 top.
cards.trigger: fires at 0.5

cards.name: The Fed cuts fast
cards.what: This tracks emergency or rapid rate cuts, which come after the panic and never before it.
cards.reading: Change in the Fed's rate over the last three months, up 0.25 points
cards.rule: It counts as fired after cuts of half a point or more in three months, and as warming after a fifth of a point.
cards.history: The Fed made a surprise cut in January 2001, an emergency three-quarter-point cut on Jan 22, 2008, and two emergency cuts to zero on March 3 and 15, 2020.
cards.trigger: fires on half a point of cuts in three months

cards.name: The Fed's balance sheet jumps
cards.what: When the Fed buys bonds or lends on a huge scale its balance sheet balloons, and that money-printing turn is usually where the inflation after a crash begins.
cards.reading: Change over the last eight weeks, with the balance sheet at $6.76 trillion
cards.rule: It counts as fired when the balance sheet grows 5% or more in eight weeks, and as warming at 2%.
cards.history: It grew 142% from September to December 2008 and 66% from March to June 2020.
cards.trigger: fires at 5% growth in eight weeks

watch.name: Fed emergency window at $22 billion two weeks running
watch.now: $9.3 billion last week and $9.2 billion the week before

watch.name: The yen strengthens fast while stocks fall
watch.now: The yen is at 159.93 per dollar and weaker by 1.1% over the last 20 trading days

watch.name: Weakest junk above 13.56 while all junk widens
watch.now: The weakest junk is at 13.16, and all junk is at 3.23, down 0.08 in a month
